claim: Goal-directed attention is usually studied by providing individuals with explicit instructions on what they should attend to.
source: Goal-directed attention is usually studied by providing individuals with explicit instructions on what they should attend to.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: In daily life, we often use past experiences to guide our attentional states.
source: But in daily life, we often use past experiences to guide our attentional states.
evidence: This is a general observation about real-world behavior.

claim: Memory-guided attention is supported by neural preparation for anticipated attentional states.
source: Given the importance of memory for predicting upcoming events, we hypothesized that memory-guided attention is supported by neural preparation for anticipated attentional states.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the study, tested through experiments.

claim: Hippocampus and mPFC exhibited higher activity for memory-guided vs. explicitly instructed attention.
source: Hippocampus and mPFC exhibited higher activity for memory-guided vs. explicitly instructed attention.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data analysis presented in the results.

claim: Representations in hippocampus and mPFC contained information about upcoming attentional states.
source: Furthermore, representations in both regions contained information about upcoming attentional states.
evidence: This is a primary finding from representational similarity analyses.

claim: In the hippocampus, preparation for upcoming attentional states was stronger for memory-guided attention.
source: In the hippocampus, this preparation was stronger for memory-guided attention, and occurred alongside stronger coupling with visual cortex during attentional guidance.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the comparison of preparatory coding between tasks.

claim: The hippocampus showed stronger coupling with visual cortex during memory-guided attention.
source: In the hippocampus, this preparation was stronger for memory-guided attention, and occurred alongside stronger coupling with visual cortex during attentional guidance.
evidence: This is a primary finding from multivariate connectivity analysis.

claim: Only a small portion of encountered information is fully processed due to limited information processing capacity.
source: Humans continuously experience rich perceptual input — input that exceeds the brain's information processing capacity (Luck and Vogel, 1997; Pylyshyn and Storm, 1988; Raymond et al., 1992). As a result, only a small portion of the information that is encountered on a moment-by-moment basis is fully processed.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on information processing capacity.

claim: Unless attended, even very salient information can go undetected.
source: Indeed, unless attended, even very salient information can go undetected (Neisser and Becklen, 1975; Simons and Chabris, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to classic studies on inattentional blindness.

claim: In laboratory studies, goal-directed attention is typically studied by providing explicit instructions to participants.
source: In laboratory studies, goal-directed attention is typically studied by providing explicit instructions to participants (Posner, 1980; Kastner and Ungerleider, 2000; Wolfe et al., 1989).
evidence: This is a characterization of the field supported by citations.

claim: Attentional states are often guided by past experiences in similar situations in daily life.
source: However, in daily life, it is exceedingly rare to receive explicit instructions on how we should direct our attention. Instead, our attentional states are often guided by past experiences in similar situations (Awh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a general observation about real-world attention supported by a citation.

claim: Memory-guided attention is effective in guiding goal-directed behavior.
source: Such memory-guided attention is effective in guiding goal-directed behavior (Aly and Turk-Browne, 2017; Chen and Hutchinson, 2018; Nobre and Stokes, 2019) but is relatively under-explored.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Interactions between hippocampus and mPFC have been linked to goal-directed behaviors guided by long-term memory.
source: Interactions between these regions have been linked to a variety of goal-directed behaviors that are guided by long-term memory (Euston et al., 2012; Kaplan et al., 2017; Shin and Jadhav, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The hippocampus contributes to attentional processing.
source: Furthermore, both the hippocampus (Aly and Turk-Browne, 2016a; Aly and Turk-Browne, 2016b; Aly and Turk-Browne, 2018; Córdova et al., 2019; Fenton et al., 2010; Mack et al., 2016; Muzzio et al., 2009; Ruiz et al., 2020) and mPFC (Mack et al., 2016; Small et al., 2003) contribute to attentional processing.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The mPFC contributes to attentional processing.
source: Furthermore, both the hippocampus (Aly and Turk-Browne, 2016a; Aly and Turk-Browne, 2016b; Aly and Turk-Browne, 2018; Córdova et al., 2019; Fenton et al., 2010; Mack et al., 2016; Muzzio et al., 2009; Ruiz et al., 2020) and mPFC (Mack et al., 2016; Small et al., 2003) contribute to attentional processing.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The hippocampus represents online attentional states.
source: Previous work from our lab has demonstrated that the hippocampus represents online attentional states (Aly and Turk-Browne, 2016a; Aly and Turk-Browne, 2016b; Córdova et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work from the authors' lab.

claim: The hippocampus plays a critical role in encoding and retrieving long-term memories.
source: Moreover, decades of work have highlighted the critical role of the hippocampus in encoding and retrieving long-term memories (Lepage et al., 1998; Shapiro and Eichenbaum, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Hippocampal activity levels are higher for memory-guided vs. explicitly instructed attention.
source: In line with this, several studies have found that hippocampal activity levels are higher for memory-guided vs. explicitly instructed attention (Aly and Turk-Browne, 2017; Stokes et al., 2012; Summerfield et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Activity enhancement for memory-guided attention in the hippocampus is present prior to attentional guidance.
source: This activity enhancement for memory-guided attention is present as soon as information from memory is available, and even prior to attentional guidance.
evidence: This is based on prior research findings cited in the text.

claim: Increased neural synchrony between hippocampus and mPFC has been observed at decision points requiring memory to guide future behavior in rodents.
source: In rodents, increased neural synchrony between the hippocampus and mPFC has been observed at decision points in which memory must be used to guide future behavior (Benchenane et al., 2010; Jones and Wilson, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior rodent studies.

claim: The orbitofrontal cortex represents goal state representations that are inferred on the basis of past experience.
source: In humans, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies have demonstrated that the orbitofrontal cortex (a region in the ventral medial prefrontal cortex) represents goal state representations that are not explicitly instructed but rather inferred on the basis of past experience (Niv, 2019; Schuck et al., 2015; Schuck et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies.

claim: The hippocampus and vmPFC show functional coupling as individuals learn which features of an object are relevant for determining its category.
source: Moreover, the hippocampus and ventromedial PFC (vmPFC) show functional coupling as individuals learn which features of an object are relevant for determining its category, and thus should be attended (Mack et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Behavioral sensitivity (A') was higher on valid trials compared to invalid trials.
source: Indeed, behavioral sensitivity (i.e., A' for detecting art or room matches) was higher on valid trials (M = 0.809, 95% CI [0.787, 0.831]) compared to invalid trials (M = 0.508, 95% CI [0.451, 0.565]), as revealed by a main effect of cue validity, F(1, 28)=128.13, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.82 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a primary behavioral finding from the experiment, shown in Figure 2.

claim: Sensitivity was higher than chance only on valid trials in the memory-guided task.
source: In fact, sensitivity was higher than chance only on valid trials (memory-guided: t(28) = 20.25, p<0.0001, d = 3.76, 95% CI [0.768, 0.828], explicitly instructed: t(28) = 26.01, p<0.0001, d = 4.83, 95% CI [0.795, 0.846]), and not on invalid trials (memory-guided: t(28) = 0.66, p=0.51, d = 0.12, 95% CI [0.412, 0.545], explicitly-instructed: t(28) = 1.08, p=0.29, d = 0.20, 95% CI [0.468, 0.606]).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Sensitivity was higher than chance only on valid trials in the explicitly instructed task.
source: In fact, sensitivity was higher than chance only on valid trials (memory-guided: t(28) = 20.25, p<0.0001, d = 3.76, 95% CI [0.768, 0.828], explicitly instructed: t(28) = 26.01, p<0.0001, d = 4.83, 95% CI [0.795, 0.846]), and not on invalid trials (memory-guided: t(28) = 0.66, p=0.51, d = 0.12, 95% CI [0.412, 0.545], explicitly-instructed: t(28) = 1.08, p=0.29, d = 0.20, 95% CI [0.468, 0.606]).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Response times were slower on invalid compared to valid trials.
source: Moreover, response times were slower on invalid compared to valid trials, F(1, 28)=76.50, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.73.
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The difference in A' between memory-guided and explicitly instructed tasks was not statistically significant.
source: We next examined behavioral performance across the memory-guided and explicitly instructed tasks, and found that the difference between them was not statistically significant (i.e., no main effect of task), F(1, 28)=3.20, p=0.084, ηp2 = 0.10.
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Decision accuracy in using stay/switch cues was high and not significantly different between 'stay' cues and 'switch' cues.
source: Decision accuracy was high and was not significantly different between 'stay' cues (M = 0.949, 95% CI [0.932, 0.955]) and 'switch' cues (M = 0.967, 95% CI [0.954, 0.978]), t(28) = 1.68, p=0.10, d = 0.31, 95% CI [−0.004, 0.040].
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from statistical analysis of the data.

claim: BOLD activity was higher for the memory-guided vs. explicitly instructed task in the hippocampus.
source: Indeed, BOLD activity was higher for the memory-guided vs. explicitly instructed task in both hippocampus, t(28) = 2.54, p=0.017, d = 0.47, 95% CI [0.872, 8.125], and vmPFC, t(28) = 3.74, p=0.0008, d = 0.69, 95% CI [2.518, 8.611] (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary fMRI finding shown in Figure 3A.

claim: BOLD activity was higher for the memory-guided vs. explicitly instructed task in vmPFC.
source: Indeed, BOLD activity was higher for the memory-guided vs. explicitly instructed task in both hippocampus, t(28) = 2.54, p=0.017, d = 0.47, 95% CI [0.872, 8.125], and vmPFC, t(28) = 3.74, p=0.0008, d = 0.69, 95% CI [2.518, 8.611] (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary fMRI finding shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The univariate activity enhancement for memory-guided attention in hippocampus and vmPFC was not related to differences in behavioral performance across tasks.
source: To determine if this difference in univariate activity is related to differences in behavioral performance across tasks, we examined whether A' differences on the memory-guided vs. explicitly instructed task predicted univariate activity differences between these two tasks, across individuals. This relationship was not statistically significant in hippocampus (R2 = 0.03, p=0.39, 95% CI [−0.502, 0.214]) or in vmPFC (R2 = 0.02, p=0.52, 95% CI [−0.470, 0.253]).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis of behavioral and neural data.

claim: The activity enhancement in hippocampus and vmPFC for memory-guided attention was strongly correlated across individuals.
source: Indeed, the activity enhancement in each region for memory-guided attention (i.e., the BOLD activity difference for memory-guided vs. explicitly instructed tasks) was strongly correlated across individuals, R2 = 0.51, p=0.000022, 95% CI [0.477, 0.867] (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The correlation between hippocampus and vmPFC activity enhancement remained significant when controlling for individual differences in behavioral performance.
source: Importantly, this correlation remained significant when controlling for individual differences in behavioral performance across tasks (R2 = 0.50, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a finding from partial correlation analysis.

claim: The hippocampus differentiated between art and room attentional states during the image period in the memory-guided task.
source: This was the case for both the hippocampus and vmPFC, in both the memory-guided (hippocampus: t(28) = 3.82, p=0.00067, d = 0.71, 95% CI [0.003, 0.009], vmPFC: t(28) = 6.58, p<0.0001, d = 1.22, 95% CI [0.009, 0.017]) and explicitly instructed tasks (hippocampus: t(28) = 7.12, p<0.0001, d = 1.32, 95% CI [0.006, 0.011], vmPFC: t(28) = 6.07, p<0.0001, d = 1.13, 95% CI [0.010, 0.021]).
evidence: This is a finding from representational similarity analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The hippocampus differentiated between art and room attentional states during the image period in the explicitly instructed task.
source: This was the case for both the hippocampus and vmPFC, in both the memory-guided (hippocampus: t(28) = 3.82, p=0.00067, d = 0.71, 95% CI [0.003, 0.009], vmPFC: t(28) = 6.58, p<0.0001, d = 1.22, 95% CI [0.009, 0.017]) and explicitly instructed tasks (hippocampus: t(28) = 7.12, p<0.0001, d = 1.32, 95% CI [0.006, 0.011], vmPFC: t(28) = 6.07, p<0.0001, d = 1.13, 95% CI [0.010, 0.021]).
evidence: This is a finding from representational similarity analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: vmPFC differentiated between art and room attentional states during the image period in the memory-guided task.
source: This was the case for both the hippocampus and vmPFC, in both the memory-guided (hippocampus: t(28) = 3.82, p=0.00067, d = 0.71, 95% CI [0.003, 0.009], vmPFC: t(28) = 6.58, p<0.0001, d = 1.22, 95% CI [0.009, 0.017]) and explicitly instructed tasks (hippocampus: t(28) = 7.12, p<0.0001, d = 1.32, 95% CI [0.006, 0.011], vmPFC: t(28) = 6.07, p<0.0001, d = 1.13, 95% CI [0.010, 0.021]).
evidence: This is a finding from representational similarity analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: vmPFC differentiated between art and room attentional states during the image period in the explicitly instructed task.
source: This was the case for both the hippocampus and vmPFC, in both the memory-guided (hippocampus: t(28) = 3.82, p=0.00067, d = 0.71, 95% CI [0.003, 0.009], vmPFC: t(28) = 6.58, p<0.0001, d = 1.22, 95% CI [0.009, 0.017]) and explicitly instructed tasks (hippocampus: t(28) = 7.12, p<0.0001, d = 1.32, 95% CI [0.006, 0.011], vmPFC: t(28) = 6.07, p<0.0001, d = 1.13, 95% CI [0.010, 0.021]).
evidence: This is a finding from representational similarity analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Hippocampal activity patterns during the orienting period resembled the upcoming attentional state more than the other attentional state in the memory-guided task.
source: Indeed, for the memory-guided task in the hippocampus (Figure 5B), activity patterns during the orienting period resembled the upcoming attentional state more than the other attentional state, t(28) = 4.78, p=0.00005, d = 0.89, 95% CI [0.008, 0.021].
evidence: This is a primary finding from preparatory coding analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Hippocampal activity patterns during the orienting period resembled the upcoming attentional state more than the other attentional state in the explicitly instructed task.
source: Unexpectedly, this effect was also observed when attention was explicitly instructed, t(28) = 2.71 p=0.011, d = 0.50, 95% CI [0.001, 0.007].
evidence: This is a finding from preparatory coding analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Preparatory attentional states in the hippocampus were stronger for the memory-guided vs. explicitly instructed task.
source: Critically, however, preparatory attentional states in the hippocampus were stronger for the memory-guided vs. explicitly instructed task, t(28) = 3.18, p=0.004, d = 0.59, 95% CI [0.004, 0.017].
evidence: This is a primary finding from comparison of preparatory coding between tasks shown in Figure 5B.

claim: vmPFC activity patterns during the orienting period resembled the upcoming attentional state more than the other attentional state in the memory-guided task.
source: In vmPFC, activity patterns during the orienting period resembled the upcoming attentional state more than the other attentional state for both the memory-guided, t(28) = 6.25, p<0.00001, d = 1.16, 95% CI [0.010, 0.019], and explicitly instructed tasks, t(28) = 4.12, p=0.00030, d = 0.77, 95% CI [0.007, 0.020].
evidence: This is a finding from preparatory coding analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: vmPFC activity patterns during the orienting period resembled the upcoming attentional state more than the other attentional state in the explicitly instructed task.
source: In vmPFC, activity patterns during the orienting period resembled the upcoming attentional state more than the other attentional state for both the memory-guided, t(28) = 6.25, p<0.00001, d = 1.16, 95% CI [0.010, 0.019], and explicitly instructed tasks, t(28) = 4.12, p=0.00030, d = 0.77, 95% CI [0.007, 0.020].
evidence: This is a finding from preparatory coding analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Preparatory attentional states in vmPFC were not significantly different between memory-guided and explicitly instructed tasks.
source: Contrary to our hypothesis, this effect was not significantly different between the tasks, t(28) = 0.77, p=0.45, d = 0.14, 95% CI [−0.003, 0.006].
evidence: This is a finding from comparison of preparatory coding between tasks shown in Figure 5B.

claim: V1-2 pattern similarity was higher for trials of the same attentional state vs. trials of different attentional states in the memory-guided task.
source: Indeed, in V1-2, pattern similarity was higher for trials of the same attentional state vs. trials of different attentional states, for both memory-guided, t(28) = 9.32, p<0.0001, d = 1.73, 95% CI [0.092, 0.144], and explicitly instructed tasks, t(28) = 11.83, p<0.0001, d = 2.20, 95% CI [0.103, 0.146].
evidence: This is a finding from representational similarity analysis of V1-2.

claim: V1-2 pattern similarity was higher for trials of the same attentional state vs. trials of different attentional states in the explicitly instructed task.
source: Indeed, in V1-2, pattern similarity was higher for trials of the same attentional state vs. trials of different attentional states, for both memory-guided, t(28) = 9.32, p<0.0001, d = 1.73, 95% CI [0.092, 0.144], and explicitly instructed tasks, t(28) = 11.83, p<0.0001, d = 2.20, 95% CI [0.103, 0.146].
evidence: This is a finding from representational similarity analysis of V1-2.

claim: Multivariate connectivity between hippocampus and V1-2 was significantly above zero in the memory-guided task.
source: Multivariate connectivity was significantly above zero in the memory-guided task, t(28) = 4.28, p=0.00020, d = 0.80, 95% CI [0.061, 0.173], but not in the explicitly instructed task, t(28) = 1.78, p=0.086, d = 0.33, 95% CI [−0.009, 0.123].
evidence: This is a finding from multivariate connectivity analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Multivariate connectivity between hippocampus and V1-2 was not significantly different from zero in the explicitly instructed task.
source: Multivariate connectivity was significantly above zero in the memory-guided task, t(28) = 4.28, p=0.00020, d = 0.80, 95% CI [0.061, 0.173], but not in the explicitly instructed task, t(28) = 1.78, p=0.086, d = 0.33, 95% CI [−0.009, 0.123].
evidence: This is a finding from multivariate connectivity analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The difference in multivariate connectivity between hippocampus and V1-2 across memory-guided and explicitly instructed tasks was statistically significant.
source: The difference between tasks was statistically significant, t(28) = 2.28, p=0.030, d = 0.42, 95% CI [0.006, 0.114].
evidence: This is a finding from comparison of multivariate connectivity between tasks shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Hippocampal univariate activity during the orienting period was not significantly different for memory-guided vs. explicitly instructed attention.
source: However, during the orienting period, univariate activity in the hippocampus was not significantly different for memory-guided (M = 14.144, 95% CI [9.123, 19.164]) vs. explicitly instructed attention (M = 17.740, 95% CI [11.077, 24.402]), t(28) = 1.28, p=0.21, d = 0.24, 95% CI [−9.369, 2.176].
evidence: This is a finding from univariate activity analysis during the orienting period.

claim: vmPFC univariate activity during the orienting period was not significantly different for memory-guided vs. explicitly instructed attention.
source: For completeness, we also examined univariate activity in vmPFC during the orienting period, but again found no significant difference between the memory-guided (M = 12.044, 95% CI [6.219, 17.870]) and explicitly instructed tasks, (M = 14.563, 95% CI [8.447, 20.678]), t(28) = 0.85, p=0.40, d = 0.16, 95% CI [−8.593, 3.556].
evidence: This is a finding from univariate activity analysis during the orienting period.

claim: No voxels survived correction for multiple comparisons when looking for regions that showed greater preparation for memory-guided vs explicitly instructed attention in whole-brain searchlight analysis.
source: No voxels survived correction for multiple comparisons (p<0.05 family-wise error corrected) when looking for regions that showed greater preparation for memory-guided vs explicitly instructed attention.
evidence: This is a finding from whole-brain searchlight analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: When analyzing only trials following a switch cue, hippocampal activity patterns during the orienting period resembled the upcoming attentional state more than the previous attentional state in the memory-guided task.
source: Indeed, when we analyzed only the trials that followed a switch cue (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), we found that hippocampal activity patterns during the orienting periods of the memory-guided task resembled the upcoming attentional state more than the other (previous trial's) attentional state, t(28) = 2.90, p=0.0072, d = 0.54, 95% CI [0.004, 0.023].
evidence: This is a finding from preparatory coding analysis of switch trials shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: When analyzing only trials following a switch cue, multivariate evidence for upcoming attentional states in the hippocampus was higher for the memory-guided vs. explicitly instructed task.
source: Finally, as in our main analysis, multivariate evidence for upcoming attentional states in the hippocampus was higher for the memory-guided vs. explicitly instructed task, t(28) = 2.85, p=0.008, d = 0.53, 95% CI [0.004, 0.023].
evidence: This is a finding from preparatory coding analysis of switch trials shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Response times to initiate the trial were on average shorter for the explicitly instructed task compared to the memory-guided task.
source: First, autocorrelation between the orienting period and image period should be higher for the explicitly instructed vs. memory-guided task because response times to initiate the trial were on average shorter for the explicitly instructed task (0.92 s vs. 1.12 s; t(28) = 2.44, p=0.021, d = 0.45, 95% CI [0.032, 0.361]).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from the experiment.

claim: Following no-cue trials, participants on average chose room more often than art in the memory-guided task.
source: Following these 'no-cue' trials, participants on average chose room (M = 16.828, 95% CI [16.299, 17.356]) more often than art (M = 14.655, 95% CI [14.144, 15.166]), t(28) = 5.90, p<0.00001, d = 1.10, 95% CI [1.418, 2.927].
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from the experiment.

claim: The hippocampus and vmPFC may work together to guide attentional behaviors on the basis of memory.
source: These findings suggest that the hippocampus and mPFC may work together to guide attentional behaviors on the basis of memory.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior findings cited in the text.

claim: The hippocampus might play an important role in establishing memory-guided attentional states.
source: These findings therefore suggest that the hippocampus might play an important role in establishing memory-guided attentional states.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior findings cited in the text.

claim: Hippocampal memories might prepare perception for attentional requirements that are anticipated based on previous experiences.
source: This suggests that the hippocampus may be using memory to direct attentional states in a preparatory fashion: Hippocampal memories might prepare perception for attentional requirements that are anticipated based on previous experiences (Stokes et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on prior research cited in the text.

claim: vmPFC might represent memory-guided attentional states.
source: Based on these studies, we predicted that vmPFC might also represent memory-guided attentional states.
evidence: This is a prediction/hypothesis based on prior research.

claim: The hippocampus and vmPFC will establish memory-based attentional states prior to when those states must be used.
source: Based on this work and the other findings noted above, we predicted that the hippocampus and vmPFC will establish memory-based attentional states prior to when those states must be used.
evidence: This is the main prediction/hypothesis of the study.

claim: These regions will prepare for upcoming attentional states primarily when they are guided by memory.
source: To this end, we first sought to determine whether these regions can differentiate between different online attentional states, and then tested whether neural signatures of these states can be detected prior to the attentional task itself — with the hypothesis that these regions will prepare for upcoming attentional states primarily when they are guided by memory.
evidence: This is a hypothesis of the study.

claim: Covariation in attentional states between the hippocampus and early visual cortex may enable mnemonically relevant information in the environment to be detected.
source: These findings raise the possibility that covariation in attentional states between the hippocampus and early visual cortex may enable mnemonically relevant information in the environment to be detected, and then acted upon, to guide behavior on the basis of memory (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the multivariate connectivity findings.

claim: The hippocampus is preferentially involved in preparing for anticipated attentional goals that are guided by memory.
source: Together, these results elucidate how the hippocampus and vmPFC support memory-guided attention, and show that the hippocampus is preferentially involved in preparing for anticipated attentional goals that are guided by memory.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The hippocampus's role in memory-guided attention may be supported via its interactions with early visual cortex.
source: Its role in memory-guided attention may be supported via its interactions with early visual cortex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the multivariate connectivity findings.

claim: Hippocampal-visual cortex interactions may be the means by which mnemonically relevant information in the environment is detected and used to guide attention and perception.
source: These interactions may be the means by which mnemonically relevant information in the environment is detected and used to guide attention and perception.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the multivariate connectivity findings.

claim: Thirty individuals from the Columbia University community participated in the study.
source: Thirty individuals from the Columbia University community participated for monetary compensation ($12/hour for behavioral sessions and $20/hour for the fMRI session; $72 in total).
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: One participant was excluded from analyses due to poor accuracy in using stay/switch cues.
source: One participant did not perform well on the memory-guided attention task, as indicated by poor accuracy in using stay/switch cues to guide attention (M = 0.847). This person's accuracy was more than three standard deviations below the group average (M = 0.954; SD = 0.0317), suggesting that they were not effectively using memory to select attentional goals. We therefore excluded this participant from the analyses, leaving 29 participants (17 female; one left-handed; all normal or corrected-to-normal vision; 18–35 years old, M = 26, SD = 4.07; 13–21 years of education, M = 17.1, SD = 2.2).
evidence: This is a description of participant exclusion criteria and final sample.

claim: The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board at Columbia University.
source: The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board at Columbia University.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Written informed consent was obtained from all participants.
source: Written informed consent was obtained from all participants.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical procedures.
